questions.q: What is Redis at its core?
options: An in-memory data structure server that holds keys mapped to typed values such as strings, lists, sets and hashes
A message broker that cannot store data
A relational database that stores tables on disk only
questions.explain: Data lives in RAM, which is why access is fast, and persistence is optional.

questions.q: Why is Redis so fast for simple commands?
options: Data is in memory and commands are executed one at a time by a single main thread without lock contention
questions.explain: Single-threaded command execution also makes each command atomic.

questions.q: What is the main cost of keeping the dataset in RAM?
options: Capacity is limited by memory, so you must plan sizing, eviction or persistence deliberately
questions.explain: Memory is more expensive than disk.

questions.q: Which is a typical Redis use?
options: Caching, sessions, counters, queues, leaderboards and rate limiting
questions.explain: It often sits beside a primary database rather than replacing it.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
SET greeting hello
GET greeting
STRLEN greeting
EXISTS greeting
EXISTS nothere
```
questions.explain: EXISTS returns the number of keys that exist; STRLEN counts bytes. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Are Redis command names case-sensitive?
options: No: commands are case-insensitive, but key names are case-sensitive
questions.explain: SET and set are the same command; user:1 and User:1 are different keys.

questions.q: What is RESP?
options: The Redis serialization protocol clients use to talk to the server
questions.explain: redis-cli speaks RESP and prints a friendly version.

questions.q: What should a healthy server answer to PING?

What does this print?
```text
SET n 10
INCR n
INCRBY n 5
DECR n
GET n
```
questions.explain: INCR on a string that holds an integer is atomic, so concurrent clients never lose updates. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q:
What does TTL return for a key with no expiry and for a missing key?
```text
SET a 1
TTL a
TTL missing
```
questions.explain: -1 means the key exists without an expiry; -2 means the key does not exist. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
SET k v EX 100
SET k w
TTL k
```
questions.explain: A plain SET overwrites the value and removes the old expiry unless you use KEEPTTL. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q:
What does SET ... NX do?
```text
SET lock a NX
SET lock b NX
GET lock
```
questions.explain: NX sets only if the key does not exist; the second call returns nil (an empty line in raw output) and the value stays a. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Why is KEYS * dangerous on a production server?
options: It scans the whole keyspace in one blocking call and stalls other clients

questions.q: What is true of SCAN?
options: It iterates incrementally using a cursor, may return a key more than once, and may miss keys added or deleted during the scan
It returns every key exactly once

questions.q: What does UNLINK do differently from DEL?
options: It removes the key immediately from the keyspace and frees the memory in a background thread

questions.q: Which key naming style is recommended?
questions.explain: Consistent prefixes make SCAN MATCH and monitoring easier.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
HSET user:1 name Ana age 30
HGET user:1 name
HINCRBY user:1 age 1
HLEN user:1
```
questions.explain: HSET returns the number of fields added. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Why use a hash for an object instead of a JSON string?
options: You can read or update single fields atomically without rewriting the whole value

questions.q: Why can HGETALL on a huge hash be a problem?
options: It returns every field in one blocking call; use HSCAN for large hashes
questions.explain: Large replies take time and bandwidth.

questions.q: Which command increments a numeric field inside a hash atomically?

What does this print?
```text
RPUSH q a b c
LPOP q
LRANGE q 0 -1
LLEN q
```
questions.explain: RPUSH + LPOP gives FIFO order; LRANGE after the pop shows b and c, so the length is 2. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Which command blocks until an item is available?
questions.explain: Workers use blocking pops to wait for jobs without polling.

questions.q: How do you keep only the latest 100 items in a list?
What is a drawback of a plain list as a job queue?
options: A popped job is gone if the worker crashes before finishing, so reliable queues use LMOVE or streams
questions.explain: Reliable patterns move the job to a processing list.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
SADD s a b c
SADD s a
SISMEMBER s b
SCARD s
```
questions.explain: Sets ignore duplicates; SADD returns the number of new members. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q:
What does SINTER return for these sets (sorted for stability)?
```text
SADD a 1 2 3
SADD b 2 3 4
SINTER a b
```
questions.explain: The intersection of {1,2,3} and {2,3,4} is {2,3}. The first two lines are the SADD counts. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Which structure fits 'unique visitors of a page'?
options: A set (or a HyperLogLog if approximate is fine)
questions.explain: Sets give exact uniqueness at a memory cost.

questions.q: What does SPOP do?

What does this print?
```text
ZADD board 100 ana 250 bo 175 cy
ZREVRANGE board 0 1 WITHSCORES
ZRANK board ana
```
questions.explain: ZREVRANGE lists highest first; ZRANK is the 0-based ascending rank of ana, who has the lowest score. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: How are members with equal scores ordered?
questions.explain: Sorted sets order by score, then member.

questions.q: Which command adds to a member's score atomically?
What are sorted sets best for?
options: Leaderboards, priority queues and time-ordered indexes
questions.explain: Skiplist plus hash give O(log N) updates.

questions.q: Why should an application create one Redis client or pool and reuse it?
options: Redis forbids more than one connection
Opening a connection per request is slow and exhausts server connections
questions.explain: Share a client or a connection pool.

questions.q: In redis-py, what does decode_responses=True do?
What should a client do when Redis is temporarily unavailable?
options: Use timeouts and retries with backoff, and decide on a fallback

questions.q: Which are well-known Node.js Redis clients?
Why use INCR to generate short-URL IDs?
options: It is atomic, so concurrent requests never get the same ID
questions.explain: Then encode the number in base62.

questions.q: How do you avoid overwriting an existing custom alias?
options: SET alias target NX and check the reply

questions.q: Where would you count clicks per short link?
options: HINCRBY on a hash or INCR on a counter key

questions.q: How do you let links expire?
options: Store a date in a hash only
Run a cron to scan all keys
Set a TTL with EXPIRE or SET ... EX

questions.q:
What encoding does a small integer string use?
```text
SET n 42
OBJECT ENCODING n
SET s hello
OBJECT ENCODING s
```
questions.explain: Integers are stored as integers; short strings use embstr. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q:
What encoding does a small hash use?
```text
HSET h a 1 b 2
OBJECT ENCODING h
```
questions.explain: Small collections use a compact listpack; large ones switch to hash tables. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: What does MEMORY USAGE key report?
options: Approximate bytes used by the key and its value
questions.explain: Use it to find expensive keys.

questions.q: Why do many small keys cost more than one hash?
options: Each key has per-key overhead; small hashes pack fields compactly

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
SETBIT visits 7 1
SETBIT visits 9 1
GETBIT visits 7
GETBIT visits 8
BITCOUNT visits
```
questions.explain: SETBIT returns the old bit value; BITCOUNT counts set bits. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Why are bitmaps good for daily active users?
options: One bit per user ID gives exact per-day sets at tiny memory, and BITOP combines days
questions.explain: User IDs must be small integers.

questions.q: What does BITOP AND do across two day bitmaps?
options: Finds users active on either day
Finds users active on both days

questions.q: What does BITFIELD let you do?
options: Read and write several fixed-width integers packed inside a string

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
PFADD v a b c a b
PFCOUNT v
PFADD v a
PFCOUNT v
```
questions.explain: HyperLogLog counts distinct elements; re-adding existing ones changes nothing. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: What is HyperLogLog's trade-off?
options: About 0.81% standard error in exchange for a fixed size of up to about 12 KB

questions.q: Can you merge HyperLogLogs?
options: Yes with PFMERGE, giving the unique count of the union
questions.explain: Useful for daily to monthly roll-ups.

questions.q: When is exact counting still necessary?
options: When you must list members or the count drives billing or security
questions.explain: Approximate for analytics, exact for money.

questions.q: Which order do GEOADD and GEOSEARCH use for coordinates?
questions.explain: A frequent source of swapped-map bugs.

questions.q:
How is geo data stored?
```text
GEOADD places 13.361389 38.115556 palermo 15.087269 37.502669 catania
TYPE places
```
questions.explain: Geo members are stored in a sorted set using a geohash as the score. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Which command finds members within a radius or box?
Can you remove a geo member with ZREM?
options: Yes, because it is a sorted set

questions.q:
What does this print for entry IDs and length?
```text
XADD s 1-1 temp 20
XADD s 1-2 temp 21
XLEN s
XRANGE s - + COUNT 1
```
questions.explain: IDs are millisecondTime-sequence; XRANGE - + returns oldest first. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: What does XADD key * field value generate?
questions.explain: Use explicit IDs only for imports.

questions.q: How do you cap a stream's memory?
How does a stream differ from a list queue?
options: It keeps entries after reading, supports IDs, ranges and consumer groups

questions.q: What does a consumer group give you?
options: Each entry is delivered to one consumer of the group, with acknowledgement tracking

questions.q: What is the pending entries list (PEL)?
options: Entries delivered to a consumer but not yet acknowledged with XACK

questions.q: A consumer crashed with unacked messages. How do other consumers take over?
options: XAUTOCLAIM or XCLAIM entries idle longer than a threshold

questions.q: Why must handlers be idempotent with consumer groups?
options: Entries can be redelivered after failures, so processing may happen more than once

questions.q: Is Pub/Sub durable?
options: No: a message is delivered only to currently connected subscribers and is not stored
questions.explain: Use streams when you need replay.

questions.q: A subscriber disconnects for a minute. What happens to messages published meanwhile?
Are keyspace notifications enabled by default?
options: No, you enable them with notify-keyspace-events
questions.explain: They also have overhead and are best-effort.

questions.q: Which command publishes a message?
questions.explain: It returns the number of receiving subscribers.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
MULTI
SET a 1
INCR a
EXEC
```
questions.explain: Commands are queued and executed together; EXEC returns one reply per command. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q:
What happens if one command in a transaction fails at runtime?
```text
SET s x
MULTI
INCR s
SET ok 1
EXEC
GET ok
```
options:
OK
OK
QUEUED
QUEUED
ERR value is not an integer or out of range

OK
1

OK
OK
QUEUED
QUEUED
OK
OK
1
questions.explain: Redis does not roll back: the failing command returns an error and the others still run. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: What does WATCH implement?
options: Optimistic locking: EXEC aborts if a watched key changed
questions.explain: Retry the transaction when EXEC returns nil.

questions.q: Are MULTI/EXEC transactions isolated from other clients' commands?
options: Yes, other commands never run in the middle of EXEC

questions.q:
What does this Lua script return?
```text
EVAL "return redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])" 1 counter 5
EVAL "return redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])" 1 counter 3
```
questions.explain: The script runs atomically; KEYS and ARGV carry key names and arguments. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Why pass key names through KEYS instead of hard-coding them?
options: So the server (and cluster) know which keys the script touches

questions.q: What is the risk of a long-running script?
options: It blocks the whole server while it runs

questions.q: How do Redis Functions differ from EVAL?
options: Functions are named, loaded libraries that persist and replicate with the data

questions.q: How would you build a leaderboard that returns the top 10 and a user's rank?
options: A sorted set with ZREVRANGE for the top 10 and ZREVRANK for the user

questions.q: Why combine a sorted set with a hash in the project?
options: The sorted set ranks IDs, the hash holds each player's details
questions.explain: Keep rank data separate from the profile.

questions.q: How would you build a bounded activity feed per user?
options: LPUSH/XADD then LTRIM or XTRIM to cap size

questions.q: When should the feed use a stream instead of a list?
options: When you need IDs, ranges by time and consumer groups

questions.q: What is the cache-aside pattern?
options: The app reads the cache first, on a miss loads from the database and writes the value into the cache
The cache is updated by the database
Writes go only to the cache

questions.q: What is write-through?
options: Writes go to the cache and the database together so the cache stays current

questions.q: Why always set a TTL on cache entries?
options: To bound staleness and memory, even if invalidation is missed

questions.q: What is negative caching?
options: Caching 'not found' results briefly to avoid repeated expensive misses

questions.q: What does maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru do when memory is full?
options: Evicts the least recently used keys from all keys

questions.q: Which policy evicts only keys that have an expiry?
options: The volatile-* policies such as volatile-lru or volatile-ttl
questions.explain: If nothing is evictable, writes fail.

questions.q: How does Redis expire keys?
options: Lazily when accessed plus an active background sample of keys with TTLs

questions.q: Is Redis' LRU exact?
options: No, it samples a few keys and approximates LRU

questions.q: What is a cache stampede?
options: Many requests miss at once for a hot key and all hit the database
questions.explain: Often when a popular key expires.

questions.q: Which technique reduces stampedes?
options: Single-flight locking or request coalescing, plus TTL jitter and early refresh
questions.explain: Only one request rebuilds the value.

questions.q: Why add random jitter to TTLs?
options: So many keys do not all expire at the same moment

questions.q: What is a clean way to invalidate many related keys at once?
options: Include a version number in the key and bump it

questions.q:
What does a fixed-window counter print?
```text
INCR rl:user1
EXPIRE rl:user1 60
INCR rl:user1
INCR rl:user1
TTL rl:user1
```
questions.explain: INCR counts requests; the EXPIRE gives the window. (TTL may read 59 on a slow machine.) Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: What is the weakness of a fixed-window limiter?
options: A client can send a burst at the end of one window and the start of the next

questions.q: How does a sliding-window limiter with a sorted set work?
options: Add each request timestamp, remove old ones with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE and count with ZCARD

questions.q: Why is a Lua script (or MULTI) useful for rate limiting?
options: The check-and-increment must be atomic or concurrent requests slip through

questions.q: What is the correct way to acquire a simple lock?
questions.explain: NX plus an expiry in one atomic command.

questions.q: Why release a lock with a script that checks the token?
options: So you never delete a lock that expired and is now held by another client
questions.explain: Compare the value, then DEL, atomically.

questions.q: What is a fencing token for?
options: A monotonically increasing number the protected resource checks so stale lock holders are rejected
questions.explain: Locks with TTLs can expire during pauses.

questions.q: When is a Redis lock NOT safe enough?
options: When correctness (not just efficiency) depends on it, because of expiry, failover and clock issues
questions.explain: Use the database or a consensus system for strict guarantees.

questions.q: How would you store a web session?
options: A hash or string under a random session ID with a TTL that refreshes on activity

questions.q: What does CLIENT TRACKING enable?
options: Server-assisted client-side caching with invalidation messages
questions.explain: The server tells the client when a key changed.

questions.q: Why is a random, unguessable session ID important?
options: Guessable IDs let attackers hijack sessions

questions.q: What belongs in a session?
options: Small identifiers and flags, not large data

questions.q: Why is LMOVE/BLMOVE useful for a reliable queue?
options: It atomically moves a job to a processing list so it is not lost if the worker crashes

questions.q: What do libraries such as BullMQ or RQ add?
options: Retries, delays, priorities and visibility into jobs on top of Redis

questions.q: How do you delay a job?
options: Store it in a sorted set scored by run time and move due jobs to the queue

questions.q: What happens to jobs that keep failing?
options: Move them to a dead-letter list after a retry limit

questions.q: What does JSON.SET let you do?
options: Store a JSON document and read or update a nested path atomically
questions.explain: Redis 8 includes JSON as part of the core.

questions.q: Why use JSON.NUMINCRBY on a path?
options: Atomically update a nested number without rewriting the document

questions.q: When is a hash a better choice than JSON?
options: For flat objects with simple fields

questions.q: How do you index JSON for queries?
options: Create a search index over JSON paths with FT.CREATE

questions.q: What does FT.CREATE do?
options: Defines a secondary index over documents with a given prefix and schema

questions.q: What is KNN vector search?
options: Finding the K stored vectors closest to a query vector

questions.q: What is the trade-off between FLAT and HNSW vector indexes?
options: FLAT is exact but scans everything; HNSW is approximate but much faster at scale
questions.explain: Pick by dataset size and recall needs.

questions.q: What must stay consistent between stored vectors and the query?
options: Dimension and embedding model (and the distance metric)

questions.q: In the API cache and limiter project, which layer should reject excess traffic?
options: The limiter, before the cache or database are touched

questions.q: How does the project avoid caching errors forever?
options: Use short TTLs for errors or do not cache them

questions.q: Why add metrics for cache hit ratio?
options: To know whether the cache is helping and tune TTLs
questions.explain: Hits divided by hits plus misses.

questions.q: What is a sensible fallback if Redis is down?
options: Serve directly from the source and fail open or closed deliberately for the limiter

questions.q: What is an RDB file?
options: A compact point-in-time snapshot of the dataset
questions.explain: Created by SAVE, BGSAVE or save rules.

questions.q: How does BGSAVE avoid blocking clients?
options: It forks a child process that writes the snapshot

questions.q: What can you lose with RDB-only persistence?
Why are RDB files good for backups and restarts?
options: They are compact and load fast

questions.q: What does appendfsync everysec risk?
options: Up to about one second of writes after a crash

questions.q: What does appendfsync always do?
options: fsync after every write command: safest and slowest

questions.q: What is an AOF rewrite?
options: Compacting the log into the shortest set of commands that rebuilds the dataset

questions.q: Why do many production setups use both RDB and AOF?
options: RDB for fast restarts and backups, AOF for better durability
questions.explain: Redis can load the AOF on restart.

questions.q: Is Redis replication synchronous by default?
options: No, it is asynchronous so a failover can lose recent writes
questions.explain: WAIT can wait for acknowledgements but does not make it strictly consistent.

questions.q: Which command makes a server a replica?
questions.explain: Use REPLICAOF NO ONE to promote.

questions.q: What does the replication backlog allow?
options: A reconnecting replica to do a partial resync instead of a full one

questions.q: Why direct reads to replicas with care?
options: Replicas can be slightly behind, so reads may be stale

questions.q: What does Sentinel do?
options: Monitors masters and replicas and promotes a replica when the master fails
questions.explain: It also tells clients the current master.

questions.q: Why run at least three Sentinels?
options: A majority must agree to avoid split-brain decisions
questions.explain: Use odd numbers on separate failure domains.

questions.q: What is the Sentinel quorum?
options: The number of Sentinels that must agree the master is down
questions.explain: A majority is still needed to authorise the failover.

questions.q: How should clients find the master with Sentinel?
options: Ask Sentinel for the current master address (use a Sentinel-aware client)

questions.q: How many hash slots does Redis Cluster have?
What does a hash tag like {user42} do?
options: Only the text inside braces is hashed, so related keys land in the same slot

questions.q: What does MOVED mean?
options: The key lives on another node; the client should update its slot map and retry there

questions.q: Why do multi-key commands need the same slot?
options: Each node only holds some slots and cannot atomically operate across nodes

questions.q: What does ASK mean during a migration?
options: The key is being moved; ask the target node once without updating the slot map

questions.q: Which tool manages cluster creation and resharding?
What should happen before removing a node?
options: Reshard its slots to other nodes, then remove it
questions.explain: An empty primary can be deleted.

questions.q: What is needed for cluster failover to work?
options: Replicas for each primary and a majority of primaries reachable

questions.q: Why never expose Redis directly to the internet?
options: It is designed for trusted networks; use a private network, auth and TLS
questions.explain: Open Redis instances are routinely abused.

questions.q: What are ACLs?
options: Per-user rules limiting commands, keys and channels

questions.q: Which is a good practice for the default user?
options: Disable it or give it a strong password and use named users with least privilege
questions.explain: Separate app, admin and replica users.

questions.q: What does TLS protect?
options: Traffic in transit between clients, replicas and nodes

questions.q: What does SLOWLOG show?
options: Recent commands that exceeded a time threshold

questions.q: Why avoid MONITOR in production?
options: It streams every command and adds significant overhead

questions.q: Which INFO fields help detect memory pressure?
options: used_memory, maxmemory, evicted_keys and fragmentation ratio

questions.q: How can you find big keys?
From the shipped license files, which license applies to Redis 7.2 and earlier?
What is Valkey?
options: A BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2.4 under the Linux Foundation

questions.q: Why can't you assume RDB files are portable between Redis and Valkey?
options: Newer versions use incompatible RDB formats

questions.q: What is a safe upgrade approach?
options: Test in staging, upgrade replicas first, fail over, then upgrade the old primary, with backups

questions.q: What is the capstone goal?
options: A production-style cluster with persistence, security, monitoring and tested failover

questions.q: Which test best proves your HA setup?
options: Kill a primary and verify automatic failover and client recovery

questions.q: What should your runbook cover?
options: Backups and restore, failover, scaling, upgrades and alerts

questions.q: Why restore from backup as a test?
options: A backup you have never restored is not proven

questions.q: Why is INCR safe for concurrent counters?
options: Redis executes each command atomically on a single thread, so two clients never read the same old value
questions.explain: Atomic commands need no client-side locking.

questions.q: You need 'unique visitors per day' for 50 million users where a 1% error is fine. Which structure?
questions.explain: Exact sets cost far more memory.

questions.q: You need 'did user 1234567 visit today' for 50 million known integer IDs, exactly. Which structure?
options: A bitmap with one bit per user ID
questions.explain: Bitmaps answer membership exactly in about 6 MB.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```text
ZADD z 5 a 5 b 3 c
ZRANGE z 0 -1
ZREVRANK z a
```
questions.explain: Equal scores are ordered lexicographically; ZREVRANK counts from the highest. Verified by running it against a real Redis 8 server.

questions.q: Which command lets you cap a stream's memory?
questions.explain: Streams are append-only logs and must be trimmed.

questions.q: A consumer in a stream group crashes before XACK. What happens to its messages?
options: They stay in the pending list and can be claimed by another consumer (at-least-once delivery)

questions.q: Why is MULTI/EXEC not a database-style transaction?
options: A runtime error in one command does not roll back the others
questions.explain: Redis queues commands and runs them without interleaving, but does not undo.

questions.q: What does WATCH do?
options: Aborts the next EXEC if a watched key was modified by another client (optimistic locking)

questions.q: Which lock acquire command is correct?
questions.explain: One atomic command with an expiry.

questions.q: Why is KEYS * banned in production?
options: It walks the whole keyspace in one blocking call; use SCAN

questions.q: What does maxmemory-policy noeviction do when memory is full?
options: Rejects write commands that need more memory
questions.explain: Choose an eviction policy for caches.

questions.q: A hot cache key expires and 5,000 requests hit the database at once. What is this and one fix?
options: A cache stampede; use single-flight locking or refresh early with TTL jitter

questions.q: What is the downside of RDB-only persistence?
options: You can lose writes since the last snapshot

questions.q: What risk does appendfsync everysec carry?
options: Up to about one second of acknowledged writes can be lost in a crash

questions.q: Why can a failover lose acknowledged writes?
options: Replication is asynchronous, so the promoted replica may not have the latest writes
questions.explain: WAIT reduces but does not remove the risk.

questions.q: Why do you need at least three Sentinels?
options: A majority must authorise a failover to avoid split-brain
questions.explain: Place them on separate failure domains.

questions.q: How are keys assigned to slots in Redis Cluster?
options: CRC16(key) mod 16384, using only the {hash tag} part if present
questions.explain: Hash tags enable multi-key operations on one node.

questions.q: What does a MOVED reply tell the client?
options: The slot lives on another node; update the slot map and retry there
questions.explain: ASK is the temporary version during migration.

questions.q: What is a safe way to protect a Redis server?
options: Private network, ACL users with least privilege and TLS, never exposed publicly

questions.q: Why should you test restoring a backup?
options: A backup that has never been restored is unproven

challenges.title: A fixed-window rate limiter in Lua
challenges.prompt: Write a Lua script that atomically counts requests per key, sets a window expiry on the first hit and allows only the first N requests. Use it for two users and inspect the counter and TTL. This runs against a real Redis server with redis-cli.
challenges.starter:
# Run these lines with redis-cli against an empty database.
# TODO: write a Lua script for EVAL that
#   1. INCRs KEYS[1]
#   2. sets EXPIRE KEYS[1] ARGV[1] seconds on the first hit only
#   3. returns 1 if the count is <= ARGV[2], otherwise 0
# Then call it 5 times for rl:ana (60 s window, limit 3), GET rl:ana,
# call it once for rl:bo, and finish with TTL rl:bo.
challenges.solution:

challenges.explain: Doing INCR, EXPIRE and the comparison inside one script makes the check-and-increment atomic, so concurrent requests cannot slip through. Calls 4 and 5 return 0 but still count, so GET shows 5. Verified by running it against Redis 8; your TTL may show 59 if a second passes.

challenges.title: A reliable job queue with LMOVE
challenges.prompt: Model a queue where a claimed job moves to a processing list, is removed when finished and is returned to the queue if the worker crashes. Run the sequence of commands and compare your output.
challenges.starter:
# Reliable queue: a job must not be lost if a worker crashes mid-job.
# 1. Enqueue j1, j2, j3 onto the list "jobs".
# 2. A worker claims two jobs by moving them to the list "processing" (oldest first, appended at the end).
# 3. Show both lists.
# 4. The worker finishes j1: remove it from "processing" and show the list.
# 5. The worker crashes while handling j2: move it back from "processing" to the end of "jobs", show "jobs".
# 6. Finish with the length of "processing".
challenges.expected:
3
j1
j2
j3
j1
j2
1
j2
j2
j3
j2
0
challenges.solution:
RPUSH jobs j1 j2 j3
LMOVE jobs processing LEFT RIGHT
LMOVE jobs processing LEFT RIGHT
LRANGE jobs 0 -1
LRANGE processing 0 -1
LREM processing 1 j1
LRANGE processing 0 -1
LMOVE processing jobs LEFT RIGHT
LRANGE jobs 0 -1
LLEN processing
challenges.explain: LMOVE is atomic, so a job always lives in exactly one list: waiting, processing or (after LREM) done. A crash leaves the job in processing, where a janitor can move it back. Verified by running it against Redis 8.
